newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan urges rebels to resume Peru hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Japan urges rebels to resume Peru hostage talks.

text.p: Japan on Friday urged Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages in Lima to reconsider their decision to boycott the next round of negotiations with the Peruvian government.
"The Japanese government strongly supports efforts by the Peruvian government and the guarantor commission to secure the safe release of all the hostages," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said.
"Therefore, we hope the the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) side will attend the next round of preliminary dialogue," he told a news conference.
On Thursday the guerrillas abruptly suspended negotiations to end the 79-day crisis saying they feared the government planned to storm the Japanese ambassador's residence where the hostages are held.
A meeting scheduled for Friday would have been the 10th round of talks since negotiations, which have been overseen by guarantors including the Canadian ambassador, began on February 11.

Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa said he had evidence the Peruvian government aimed to try to rescue the hostages while he and his second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, attended negotiations at a safehouse across the street from the diplomatic residence.
"We have been hearing noises from underneath the floor of the house," Cerpa said, hinting that he believed Peruvian security forces were digging tunnels to enter the residence.
At the last round of talks on Wednesday the government presented the MRTA with what President Alberto Fujimori called an "all-inclusive" proposal for a peaceful end to the siege.
Cuba's President Fidel Castro on Monday accepted Fujimori's request to grant asylum to the 20-odd guerrillas holding the hostages if the two sides reach an accord.
But the rebels reacted unenthusiastically to the idea.
The rebels stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence on December 17 and seized hundreds of cocktail party guests.

They released most in the following weeks. Among those still held are Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two government ministers, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
